1.goal: To open by saying why the exam format is here.
run: Say out loud that this is not a mock exam. She asked for the TOEFL in the first lesson; the format is here because it is the most demanding short-presentation genre there is, and because it calls on everything in the block at once.
This is the fourth lesson of the block and the one that closes it. Today's post-lesson record steers the planning that follows — keep the last two minutes for it.
1.expected: That she treats it as a presentation under a clock, not as a test.
1.support: If she reads it as assessment, say what happens with the recordings: they are evidence for planning, not a score.
1.challenge: Ask which of the four lessons in the block she expects to draw on most in forty-five seconds.
1.monitoring: Whether exam anxiety changes how she speaks. If it does, that is worth recording — it will come back at the real exam.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The samples start at stage 3.
1.transition: Move on when she understands it is a presentation under a clock, not a test.

2.goal: To establish the rules of the game before any attempt.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the task on screen together.
run: Read the task with her.
Confirm: fifteen seconds to DECIDE, not to write; forty-five to speak; the clock does not stop.
Do not give structure tips here. The attempt at stage 3 counts as diagnostic, and it is worth more without scaffolding.
2.expected: That she knows the three rules and asks nothing further.
2.support: If she wants to write during the fifteen seconds, say the format does not allow it and that deciding is the work.
2.challenge: Ask what she would do with the fifteen seconds if she could plan them now.
2.monitoring: Whether she is already building structure before being asked to. It contaminates the diagnostic — say the rules and move.
2.transition: Move on when she knows the rules.

3.goal: To see what she produces BEFORE any model. This is diagnostic.
3.interaction: T reads the prompt and times; S speaks alone. No help.
run: Read the prompt out loud, time fifteen seconds, then forty-five. Time it for real.
Do not help, do not finish her sentence, do not suggest.
If she explains both sides before choosing, let it happen. It is the most likely thing to work on, and the whole lesson depends on her hearing herself do it.
exact: Only the clock, and nothing else: “Fifteen seconds to think.” … “Now, forty-five seconds. Start.” … “Time.”
3.expected: Whatever she has. Very likely: both sides explained before the position arrives.
3.support: None here. Anything you add contaminates the baseline.
3.challenge: None here, for the same reason.
3.monitoring: NOTE: the second in which the position appears, and whether she reached a close. Those are the two numbers the lesson that closes the block uses.
3.evidence: The two numbers, and her own self-marking. They are the first free-production sample of the cycle.
3.transition: Move on when the attempt and the self-marking are done.

4.goal: To hear an answer that works, AFTER having tried.
4.interaction: S listens, then T–S against her own attempt.
run: Play the model answer.
Ask: in which second did the position arrive? How many reasons? Where is the concession?
The comparison is with HER attempt, not with an ideal. Go back to the self-marking from stage 3.
exact: Did he explain both sides before choosing? (No.) Why did he not need to? (The prompt already explained them.)
4.expected: The position early, two reasons, one concession, and a close that does not repeat the reasons.
4.support: If the structure is hard to hear, play it again and ask her to raise a hand at the second the position arrives.
4.challenge: Ask what she would cut from the model to fit thirty seconds.
4.monitoring: Whether she compares herself to the model or to an ideal. Only the first is useful.
4.evidence: The difference she names between her attempt and the model.
4.transition: Move on when she points at the difference between her answer and the model.

5.goal: To name the five moves of the model answer.
5.interaction: S classifies alone, then T–S on what she skipped.
run: She classifies, then open the explanation.
Ask which of the five she skipped in her own attempt.
The four-second concession is the move from lesson 5, now at speed. Name the link out loud.
exact: Does the close repeat the reasons? (No.) What does it do? (It takes the position back up, after weighing them.)
5.expected: Position, two reasons, a concession and a close — with the fifth being the one she skipped.
5.support: If the close and the position blur, read the two lines back to back and ask what the second one adds.
5.challenge: Ask her to say the five moves in order, with no example, as a checklist she could use in fifteen seconds.
5.monitoring: Whether she recognizes the concession as the same move as lesson 5. The link is what makes it reachable at speed.
5.evidence: Which of the five she names as the one she skipped.
5.transition: Move on when she names the five.

6.goal: To automate the openings, without the whole argument.
6.interaction: T gives a topic in two words; S gives back the first eight seconds only. Eight rounds.
run: You say a topic in two words, she gives back ONLY the first eight seconds — position plus “mainly for two reasons”.
Eight rounds in seven minutes. Do not let it turn into a full answer.
Pronunciation: “I would say” comes out as one thing, almost “I'd say”. If she separates the three words, she has already spent a second of the eight.
6.expected: Eight openings, each with the position and the announcement of two reasons.
6.support: If the position will not come, give the topic again with two options and let her pick one out loud.
6.challenge: Give a topic she disagrees with and ask for the opening anyway.
6.monitoring: How long the position takes, and whether it shortens across the eight.
6.evidence: How many of the eight come out under eight seconds. It is the measure of access.
6.transition: Move on when the position comes out in under eight seconds three times in a row.

7.goal: Four timed answers, on new prompts.
7.interaction: T reads and times; S answers. Four in a row, no comments in between.
run: Read the prompt, time 15s, time 45s. No help, no second chance, no comment between one and the next. All four in a row.
Do not comment between the answers. The value of round one is her hearing her own consistency — and you having four comparable samples for the lesson that closes the block.
7.expected: Four answers, each with a position, reasons and a close inside the time.
7.support: None between answers. Everything goes to stage 8.
7.challenge: None here — the constraint is already the challenge.
7.monitoring: NOTE per answer: the second the position appeared, the number of reasons, whether there was a concession, and whether she closed inside the time.
7.evidence: The four sets of numbers. They are the comparable samples the block closure reads.
7.transition: Move on when the four are done.

8.goal: To hand back the NUMBERS, not impressions.
8.interaction: T–S over the four sets of numbers, then one decision.
run: Say the four seconds at which the position appeared, and how many closed inside the time.
Then choose ONE thing to improve in round two. One only — two is already more than fits in forty-five seconds of attention.
If she explained both sides in any of the four, that is the thing. The prompt has already explained both sides.
8.expected: One adjustment, named by her, in one sentence.
8.support: If she cannot choose, read the four numbers again and ask which one she would rather change.
8.challenge: Ask her to say how the first eight seconds will sound with the adjustment, before round two.
8.monitoring: Whether the adjustment she picks is the one the numbers point at, or the one she feels worst about.
8.evidence: The adjustment chosen. It is what round two tests.
8.transition: Move on when she knows what the single adjustment is.

9.goal: Two new answers with the single adjustment applied.
9.interaction: T reads and times; S answers. Two prompts.
run: Two new prompts, same clock.
Then compare the numbers with round one, out loud.
Stop at six minutes. The last two are for the close and for the block record.
9.expected: The same structure with the adjustment holding under the clock.
9.support: If the adjustment disappears in the first one, name it once before the second and time it again.
9.challenge: Ask for a third prompt at thirty seconds if the two came out clean.
9.monitoring: Whether the adjustment survived the clock. An adjustment that only appears when she is thinking about it is not an adjustment yet.
9.evidence: The two sets of numbers against round one. Both go in the record.

10.goal: To close the block and to record the three things the next block is planned from.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on one question that has to be asked today.
run: She ticks what she recognizes.
Ask her, today, WHICH CAMBRIDGE EXAM. B2 First and C1 Advanced measure different things and change block 3 onwards. This is settled by asking, not by inferring.
Say that the next block starts from this record, and do not promise a topic.
exact: The question that cannot wait: “Which Cambridge exam are you aiming at — B2 First or C1 Advanced?”
10.expected: One answer about the exam, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If she does not know which exam, ask what the certificate is for. The purpose decides the level.
10.challenge: Ask which of the four lessons in the block she would repeat, and why that one.
10.monitoring: Whether the confidence row matches the numbers from round two. A gap either way belongs in the record.
10.evidence: THIS LESSON CLOSES BLOCK 1. Today's record is read together with lessons 3, 4 and 5 and steers three things: (1) signposting — whether the difficulty was signposting the reasoning rather than the form; if the six recordings show signposting under the clock, block 2 moves up to argument under challenge. (2) The production band — the level. Today's samples are her first recorded free production; the file says B1 and the evidence points higher. (3) The target exam, answered by her today.
10.transition: Close the lesson, and the block.
